Camera or scanner capture,

Download View source

macOS 14.0 or later · Apple Silicon and Intel · Apache-2.0

negaflow imports film captured with a scanner or digital camera and develops it on macOS. Its development engine is called Chroma Engine, and its dust and scratch restoration system is called GrainMend. The entire process is developed independently and brings film development, adjustment, and output into one app.

Defect restoration

GrainMend

GrainMend RGB is an independently developed software method that detects and restores dust, pinholes, scratches, and emulsion damage without an infrared channel.

Read more

GrainMend RGB

GrainMend RGB Defect Restoration

Guided and Brush: about 1 second · Auto: 5–10 seconds Compared with the 30–90 seconds typically required for a hardware IR pass, GrainMend RGB is about 3–90× faster.

Before After

negaflow warns you when false detections become likely.

Auto

Finds and restores defects across the photograph.

Guided

Finds defects inside an area you specify.

Brush

Paints the area to restore directly.

Clone Stamp

Copies pixels from a selected source to another location.

Detection that rivals hardware IR

GrainMend RGB detects defects directly in the RGB image and checks nearby texture, direction, and structure before restoring them. Lines and grids in the photograph are kept separate from scratches.

Review and correct it yourself

Inspect the detection mask and restored result yourself, then correct the affected area as needed.

Non-destructive layers

Each GrainMend RGB layer can be adjusted in strength, inspected as a mask, disabled, or deleted separately.

False-detection warning

GrainMend alerts the user when false-detected areas are likely to occur.

GrainMend IR

GrainMend IR is an optional path when the scanner plugin provides an infrared channel. Its detection result is added to the same edit history as GrainMend RGB.

GrainMend RGB is an independently developed software method, separate from hardware infrared cleaning. GrainMend IR uses the scanner’s infrared channel; it is not an implementation or compatibility mode of Digital ICE, iSRD, or SRDx.

Cyanotype, glass plate and gelatin silver are made to look the part. They are not measured from real chemistry, plates or paper.

Printer ICC Profile Matching

Supports sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB, and custom RGB printer ICC profiles.

Non-destructive Print Layouts

Borders are set the way you would set them in a darkroom, and the page renders to high-resolution 16-bit TIFF.

Color Mathematics

32-bit Float Linear Pipeline

Inversion and tone are computed in 32-bit float linear space prior to gamma encoding, minimising clipping and tone degradation.

Dmin Density Inversion

Density D = log₁₀(Dmin/T) is calculated from linear transmittance and unexposed base measurements.

Stretched Exponential Curve

Applies a dedicated print response curve with an exact inverse function derived from four reference points.

Decoupled Processing

Film emulsion properties, scan light source, and scanner target looks are evaluated in separate stages.

Output Color Space Management

Converts to sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB, or custom RGB Printer ICC profiles at the final display and export stages.

48-bit RGB (16-bit per Channel) Precision

Supports full 48-bit RGB (16-bit R/G/B, 281 trillion colors) input and output, which keeps posterization and banding down through heavy tonal adjustment.

Lossless Archival Output

Pairs 48-bit I/O with 32-bit float linear processing, leaving headroom for film archiving and large prints.

Film profiles

Film Stock Calibration Dataset

Read more

928 Image observations
15 Bundled scanner profiles

The bundle contains 15 scanner profiles made from film material I photographed myself. The profiles record 928 image observations, and every profile is currently marked realOnly.

realOnly identifies a profile built from real scans and still under active development and refinement. More scan material from a wider range of films and equipment will be added, and the profiles will continue to expand and improve with it.

Profiles are never applied from the scanner name alone; the user selects one explicitly. SHA-256 hashes are provided for both the files and the list.

928 is the sum of the observations in each profile, not 928 distinct photographs. The same film can be counted for more than one scanner. The scans were reviewed directly, files with false detections were excluded, and the profiles were built from those measurements.

Comparison

A free, open-source alternative to paid film inversion software

Film inversion is usually done with a Lightroom plug-in (Negative Lab Pro and the like), a paid standalone app (FilmLab, Negbase and others), or the software that comes with a scanner (SilverFast, VueScan). negaflow is a free, open-source macOS app that does the whole job on its own — inversion, development, dust and scratch repair, print and export.

Guide

Scanning film with a digital camera

Faster than a flatbed and, with a decent macro lens, sharper. The rig, the alignment, the capture settings, and where the raw files go next.

Read more

The rig

A camera that shoots raw, a macro lens that reaches 1:1, a film holder, a light pad, and a copy stand or tripod to hold the camera above it. Getting to 1:1 with extension tubes or bellows costs you flat field, and the corners go soft.

Light

Diffused, CRI 95 or higher, 5000–5500K. Below that the colour will not come back after inversion, and no amount of grading fixes it. Lift the film a few millimetres off the pad so surface dust and the LED grid fall out of the focal plane. If the pad flickers, stay slower than 1/60s.

Alignment

The sensor plane has to be parallel to the film, or only part of the frame is in focus. The reliable way: put a small mirror on the light pad and adjust the camera until the reflection of the lens sits dead centre in live view. A spirit level only tells you anything if the tripod column is truly vertical.

Flatness

Curled film loses the edges. Hold it in a film holder, or between anti-Newton glass. Plain glass gives you Newton rings.

Capture settings

Base ISO, f/5.6–f/8, manual focus with live view magnified. Stopping down further costs sharpness to diffraction. Use a remote release or the 2-second timer, and the electronic shutter on mirrorless. Shoot raw and keep the right end of the histogram off the wall — that end is the film base.

Developing

Open the raw files in negaflow and the film base is found for you: it groups connected regions in the brightness distribution and drops sprocket holes, the holder and bare backlight. If the result is off, sample unexposed film with the eyedropper or type the RGB in.

Guide

How to invert a film negative

There is a reason the colour goes muddy when you flip a curve. Three separate things have to happen: the orange mask is divided out, the inversion runs in linear light, and a print curve goes on top.

Read more

1. Measure the film base (Dmin)

The orange mask is a filter over the whole frame. Measure it on unexposed film rather than inside the picture, or that frame's own colour ends up in the mask. negaflow finds it by grouping connected regions in the brightness distribution; the eyedropper and direct RGB entry are there too.

2. Divide, do not subtract

The mask is a transmission, so it divides out in linear light. D = log₁₀(Dmin/T). Subtract it from a gamma-encoded 8-bit image instead and the channels come apart — that is the crossed colour everyone knows.

3. Invert in linear

Invert after gamma and the shadows are the first thing to block up. negaflow finishes the inversion and the tone work in 32-bit float linear, then hands off to the output colour space.

4. Print response curve

A negative has no black and no white of its own. Photographic paper decided those. A curve anchored on black, 18% grey and white is what makes the result read as a photograph.

5. Keep the roll together

One base measurement covers a roll shot under one light. Set it per frame and the tone wanders across the roll. Carry one value through all of them and correct exposure frame by frame.

6. Pick a look, then export

The development targets stand in for lab scans from a Frontier or a Noritsu. 16-bit TIFF if you are carrying on editing, JPEG with the roll's EXIF written in if you are not.

Pro Pipeline & Productivity

Lab Workflows for Batch Digitizing

Batch Copy & Paste Scope

Batch process entire 36-exposure rolls with selective development adjustment copy & paste, keyboard nudges, and immediate pipeline sync.

Dedicated Negative, Slide & B&W Pipelines

Separate rendering pipelines for Color Negative, Positive Slide (Dmax), and B&W films—preserving tone without unwanted color shifts.

Decoupled Light Source & Emulsion Calibration

Decouples LED backlight color temperature from film base measurements, ensuring consistent inversion across different scanners and light pads.

Roll-Level Neutral Balance

Evaluates unexposed base and neutral axis statistics across an entire roll to keep color and tone even across all frames.

Advanced Precision & Library Tools

Archival & Library Precision Control

Offline Media Thumbnail & Preview

Inspect thumbnails and preview renders immediately even when external drives or NAS storage are disconnected.

SQLite FTS Metadata Search

Instantly search thousands of film frames by camera, lens, film stock, date, and user tags.

IT8.7/2 Scanner Target Profiling

Calibrate scanner sensor and light source color distortions using IT8.7/2 targets for exact color accuracy.

Atmospheric Haze Removal

Selectively suppresses fog and haze on aged film negatives without destroying original sharpness or grain structure.

B&W Split-Toning & Chemical Toning

Dedicated B&W toning engine supporting highlight/shadow split-toning, Sepia, Selenium, and Cold Tone rendering.

Fixed Sensor Dust Suppression

Automatically suppresses vertical streaks caused by fixed sensor dust on scanner glass across an entire roll.

Custom Export Templates & Presets

Configure export presets and dynamic file naming rules such as {film}_{date}_{roll}_{num}.

Native macOS Theme Sync

Follows the macOS Light and Dark modes and observes native system accessibility standards.

Settings

  • Film-base measurement and colour or black-and-white film inversion
  • Exposure, contrast, curves, HSL, colour grading, and black-and-white toning
  • Sharpening, noise reduction, grain, vignette, and halation
  • Rolls, folders, collections, ratings, stacks, and virtual copies
  • Zoom, crop, rotate, compare, histogram, and clipping indicators
  • JPEG and 16-bit TIFF export, ICC profiles, and print layouts

Basic workflow

  1. Import image files or scan with an installed plugin.
  2. Choose the development process and target.
  3. Adjust colour and tone in Chroma Engine.
  4. Apply GrainMend to photographs that need it.
  5. Check the result with Compare and the histogram, then print or export.
  6. It is built to be easy to use. Shortcuts, folder paths, presets, and adjustments can all be customised.

negaflow-scanner-sane

negaflow-scanner-sane is the plugin used by Scanner Import in negaflow.

View on GitHub ↗

Analog photography is growing again, but the process behind it has stalled.Unless film is printed optically, it has to be converted to digital before we can see it.Yet that whole process is slowing down as labs close and support from manufacturers and products declines.

This project began with the things that felt inconvenient and the features I wished existed.Drawing on what I learned from using 35mm and medium-format film, I built the entire process myself, one piece at a time.It began as a toy project for my own use, but negaflow has become something more.

What matters most is that it works well, is comfortable and fast to use, and produces a proper result.The independently developed negaflow is native to macOS and brings together workflows for both film labs and individuals.

For the summer of the 200th anniversary of the first photograph made by Niépce.

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I open the app if macOS shows a developer warning?

Current GitHub release files are ad-hoc signed. If macOS blocks the first launch, navigate to System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway.

Can I connect a physical scanner (e.g. Epson) directly?

Physical scanner connection requires the separate open-source negaflow-scanner-sane plugin. Without the plugin, you can immediately develop camera copy files or existing scans (TIFF, JPEG, RAW).

Does negaflow support camera RAW files and 16-bit TIFF?

Yes, it supports all camera RAW formats handled by macOS Image I/O, as well as 8-bit/16-bit TIFF, JPEG, and PNG files.

Are original image files modified during editing?

No. negaflow is non-destructive. Original files and third-party sidecars are never modified; all edits are stored in an independent SQLite catalog.

Does negaflow support both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs?

Yes, negaflow is distributed as a Universal PKG for both Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) and Intel Macs, requiring macOS 14.0 or later.

Can I use negaflow alongside Photoshop or Lightroom?

Yes. You can export 16-bit TIFF or JPEG files with preserved EXIF metadata and seamlessly pass them to Lightroom, Photoshop, or Capture One.

Do I need the scanner plugin for digital camera scans?

No. The plugin is only required for controlling physical flatbed or film scanners. Digital camera copies (RAW/TIFF) can be developed out of the box.

Is negaflow a subscription or open-source software?

negaflow is open-source software under the Apache License 2.0. It is completely free to download and use with no monthly subscription fees. It is free. Free as in it costs nothing, and free as in you can read the source, change it and pass it on — just keep the licence and the notices, and say what you changed. The name is a separate matter — Apache 2.0 does not grant trademark rights.

How does negaflow handle large libraries with hundreds of frames?

negaflow uses an SQLite database with WAL mode and automatic frame cache relief, ensuring stable, fluid performance across thousands of photos.

Can I save custom development presets or copy settings across rolls?

Yes. You can save custom presets or use Settings Paste Scope to selectively copy exposure, tone, or dust restoration adjustments to entire 36-exposure rolls.
